Mr. Editor. Sir ! Should you have no interesting news pr: Packet to oiler your readers, you may perhaps find a corner in your paper for the following local remarks : A great Statesman, observed, þÿ that the severest Judge, though he chastises, also hears the þÿparty. This being in accordance with reason, I am encouraged to make this public appeal, with the hope that it may tend to ultimate good. The Retailers of the Necessaries of life, (particularly Bread) may well be expected to lift up their voices, and cry aloud to be heard, if they are not permitted to vend the same, to that portion of the Inhabitants (the Peasantry) who being the most numerous, arc the surest and best Cash customers. Saturday being market or fair day, it was ever customary for the venders of Bread and Provisions, to marshall themselves (not in military) but, trading array at their stalls, with the pleasing hope of reaping a golden harvest, in which they were seldom disappointed, as they were permitted By the old regulations to keep the position or stand , from early dawn until sunset þÿ Now

\ri:u, issi. mark ! this was in the days when slavery existed, not a century ago, but only within a few short years past þÿ in the good old times, when the Baker and Retailer, could punctually meet their engagements. Now a blightening change is experienced, by this toiling and necessary class, by those baneful new local Enactments, which sweep them, their country customers, and all the good things that sustain life, out of the market-place, with one fell swoop as if by magic, leaving not a vestige behind, at the early hour of 4 þÿo clock. The necessity no longer exists, of the Peasants, leaving the market at an early hour in order that they should attend to that essential duty of throwing grass, or furnishing fodder for the stock, on Saturday evening, as the Provisional Act of the 20th January 1849 parag: 7 expressly declares, þÿ that no throwing of grass or wood, shall he exacted during extra þÿhours. As they now seldom enter the town on Saturdays, before mid-day, with their ground Provisions, A:c. for market, being obliged to remain late on the Estate on that day, in order to receive their weekly wages ; the market sales, only commencing at 2 þÿo clock.This class of individuals, having not sufficient time, from that hour to 4 þÿo clock to effect sales, still less to make their full purchases from the poor dependent Retailers. The result need not he told, as it is both seen, and severely felt, through all the ramifications of trade. The poor Peasant finds that he has travelled miles

in vain þÿ the wife and children of the artizan (who receives his pay from his employer at 4 þÿo clock)finds they arc too late for market, and that their small means is rendered useless. þÿ The Baker and Retailer are driven to their homes, with their packs, there to cogitate at leisure, how they are to face, or escape duns, (particularly at this season) on that fearful day þÿ blue Monday. þÿ The Merchants and Danish Captains are also sufferers, as they may expect nothing but disappointment in their collections, many of their debtors, being spirited away in consequence of their light purses. These evils, will find a speedy remedy, if properly represented, as we may sanguinely hope that the chief Magistrate will not permit a continuance ot this distressing order ofthings, dooming the town inhabitants in particular, to poverty and ruin. Your þÿobed servant, t. A RETAILER Christiansted 24tli April 1851

From the St. Thomas Times, April 20. Centrifugal Machines. Messrs. Candler anil Alexander, from the Society of Friends, who travelled in the West Indies last year, and have now published their Report in the Anti- Slavery Reporter , speaks in the following terms of the wonders of the þÿ þÿCentrifugal, which had then just been imported into Jamaica : þÿ þÿ On one of these estates, near Spanish Town, we saw in operation a Centrifugal Cylinder, for curing sugar, the simplicity and effectiveness of which pleased us greatly By means of a swift rotary motion, the sugar, as it comes from the coolers, is thrown against a liningofperforated metal ; the molasses are thus immediately separated from the mass, and the pure crystallised sugar alone remains. To cure sugar in the ordinary way, by putting it into hogsheads, is a process of weeks ; the cylindrical operation performs it in fifteen minutes ! Sugar ordinarily looses much of the remaining molasses by draining on ship-board. þÿ By this new mode of curing, it has none to loose and thus a great saving is effected. This was the lirst and only machine of the kind in Jamaica, or so far as we know, in all the West Indies. It w;.s about to be introduced on another large estate belonging to the same proprietor, in the North of the Island, and will probably soon become general. The machinery, and its cost of erection, scarct ly exceeds £200 sterling ; and the whole process is so plain and simple, þÿ that a child may understand þÿit. We understand that a few of these
very ingeniously constructed Machines, destined for St. Groix, have lately been landed here, and can be seen at Messrs. P. Smith A þÿCo. wharf. s

MEXICO AND SOUTH AMERICA (Harper's Magazine for April.) Sefior Mungnia, the new Bishop of Michoacan, has refused to take the oaths required by Government, throwing himself upon the rights and privileges granted to the clergy, upon the first establishment of Christianity in Mexico. Great complaints arc made of the inefficiency of the police in the capital. On the 3d of January a band of armed robbers attacked the promenaders on the I'asco, riding them of their money and valuables. Chihuahua was greatly alarmed by the report that a hand þÿol American adventurers and Indians were encamped at a distance of 25 leagues. þÿ The band is said to be well armed, having two field-pieces. From the description of the leader he is supposed 'o be the notorious Captain French. The affairs of Yucatan arc in a situation almost desperate. The Indians are waging fierce hostilities, which have prevented the transportation of provisions. The treasury is exhausted, the army without pay, and almost reduced to starvation. A poetical work, by voting Mexican woman, is advertised 1' is entitled the þÿ Awakener of Patriot

þÿ- AL'-l 11 JLiL'U'i --- ism," and narrates the history of the late war with the United States. Hostilities have broken out between the central Government of Guatemala on the one hand, and the allied States of San Salvador and Honduras on the other. A battle took place on the 21st of January at a village called San Jose, when the forces of San Salvador and Honduras were totally routed, and fled in every direction, closely pursued by the victors. Such, at least, is the Guatemalan account, which is the only one that has yet reached us. Attention has recently been turned to the gold region of New Grenada, portions of which have been found to be extremely productive. The districts richest in gold are said to be extremely unhealthy. From Nicaragua we learn that the survey of the route from Lake Nicaragua to the Pacific is nearly completed. The distance is 12 miles, and the highest point only 40 feet. The steamer Director is running on the lake. A complete steam communication will in a few weeks be effected between the lake and the Atlantic; a canal of 12 miles will unite the lake with the Pacific. When lines of steamers are established on both sides of the Isthmus, connecting with this route across, it is anticipated that the passage from New York to San Francisco may be made in 24 days. Carthagena was visited on the 7th of February by a severe shock of an earthquake, which lasted nine seconds. Considerable damage was done throughout the city; some houses were thrown down, and several lives lost. The city-

walls and the Cathedral were much injured. Had the shock been protracted a few seconds longer, the whole city would have been laid in ruins. On the flight of the 8th the public squares and walks were filled with people who had left their dwellings in dread of a repetition of the shock. Hut up to the 15th none had occurred. No city in the region felt the shock so severely as did Carthagena. In Peru, Congress was to meet March 20. The Presidential election has terminated in favor of Echenique. In Bolivia there have been one ortw-o attempts at insurrection. A decree has been issued, banishing all Buenos Ayreans except those married to Bolivian women, and all who were known as Federalists. From Brazil it is officially announced that liberated slaves, not Brazilian born, must not be taken to that country. By a law of 1831, which it is announced will be rigidly enforced, a penalty of 100 milreas, besides expenses of re-exportation, is imposed upon masters of vessels for each such person landed.

FUGITIVE SLAVE. A good deal of excitement was created by the rescue at Boston of a person laimed and arrested as a fugitive slave, under the law of the last session. The rescue was effected by a mob, mainly of colored men, who rushed into the room

i. a <0 IB <0 It S£ ATI s where the alleged fugitive was in custody of the officers, took him therefrom, and started him on his way to Canada, where he safely arrived soon after. Intelligence of the affair was transmitted by telegraph to Washington. The President issued a proclamation, commanding obedience to the laws, and sent a message to Congress, narrating the facts, and stating that the whole power of the Government should be used to enforce the laws. The matter was referred to the Judiciary Committee in the Senate, from which two reports were made þÿ ships, one by Mr. Bkadrukv, of Maine, stating that the President possessed all needful power, and the other from Mr. Butler, of South Carolina, arguing that the President could not call out either the army and navy or tiie militia to suppress an insurrection, without having previously issued a proclamation. No further action upon the subject was had in Congress, hut a great number of arrests have been made in Boston of persons charged with participation in the rescue. þÿ Ibid.

A cool attempt to swindle the treasury out of £20,090 has been made in behalf of the estate of the late Queen Dowager. Her comfortable annuity of £100,000 was made payable at regular quarter-days, commencing after the death of William IV. As it happened, he died ten days before the quarter-day, so that the queen received pay for a whole quarter for those ten days. She died 63 days after the last quarterly payment ; and a j claim was made for payment for that | time ; although blending the two periods together she would have received a þÿquarter payment s for 19 days less than a þÿquarter s time. The court, however, refused to grant the privilege of burning the candle at both ends ; and the beggarly German heirs of the late queen fail in gaining the sum. Petitions have been presented to Parliament from the bishop, commissioners of parishes, and house-holders of Capetown, stating that the Legislative Assembly of tbe colony has lost the confidence of the colonists, and presenting the details of a constitution which they pray may be granted them. The proposed abolition of the Viceroyalty in Ireland, excites great opposition, especially in Dublin. A large meeting has been held, at which the Lord Mayor presided, for the purpose of petitioning against the intended abolition, and protesting against the system of centralization which, it is alleged, has been so destructive of the best interests of Ireland. þÿ Ibid.

Among the curiosities of industry which will be displayed at the Exhibition will be a silver teakettle, manufactured out of a four penny piece by a working man. This minute specimen of workmanship weighs only about the eighteenth part of on ounce, and is quite þÿperfect. Belfast News Letter, March 12.

No alteration in the political condition of Holstein had been proposed or thought of previous 1839. Mon- to over, the people of this duchy did not in the least wish for it; and indeed the prosperity of Holstein was the most striking evidence of the liberal administration of the Danish government. The natural and intellectual resources of the country had been freely allowed to improve, and no attempt had ever been made to infringe upon the liberties of the people, or to supplant the German language by the Danish. Rut there were in Holstein and Sleswiek some lawyers, almost clientless, who being unable to subsist by their profession, for this reason had long desired to make a living in some other way. It would lead us too far, were we to all the intrigues and machinations employed by the lawyers and their friends to instigate the quiet and happy people in the duchies to sever the ties connecting them with Denmark. All their exertions, however, would have been frustrated by the sound sense of the people, had not the revolutions in in 1848 come to their assistance. Of course, they had been in the moral necessity to allege an ostensible. motive of their exertions; and for this

purpose they brought upon the tapis the fact, that the presumptive heir of the Danish crown, present (since the 20th of January, 1848) reigning king, Frederic VI J. , lias hitherto been without children, and the jmsibiliti / that he may die without any. In this case the Danish throne would be inherited by a female line ; and now those instigators pretend that not a female but a male line of succession, and therefore especially the grand duke of Oldenburg, is entitled to the inheritance of Holstein. (The claims of the dukes of Sonderburjr-Augustenburg and of Glucksburg have in substance only reference to Slesvvick.) The futility of this pretension is evinced first by the fact that King Christian I., in t l >i), inherited Holstein not bv the right of his father, but by the right of his mother; and secondly by the fact, that Holstein was from the years 1481 and 1533 until 1773 not an independent hereditary duchy, but a fee of the Vanish ermrn, and escheated, to it in the last-named year. That all their public resources have been ruined, their trade and commercial intercourse interrupted, their ports blockaded, the exportation of cattle, horses and other productions reduced to nothing, ari l their agricultural enterprises in general paralyzed, has already been alluded to above. In the second place, the people in the duchies have sustained incalculable direct losses, by

feeding the German troops and a host of adventurers, by paying war-taxes, and by ravages and devastations of foreigners. The resources of the duchies have until the commencement of the war been almost inexhaustible; but if these disasters continue, there will at last re- " main nothing more to be lost. hat, then, will all these losses have For been sustained? THE CRYSTAL PALACE. In the early months of last year the Great Exhibition had become as nearly a þÿ fixed þÿfact as any thing in the future can be. The place where and the building in which it was to be held, then became matters for grave consideration. þÿ The first point, fortunately, presented little difficulty, the south side of llydepark, betw een Kensington-road and Rotten-now, having been early selected a« the locality. The construction of the edifice, however, presented difficulties not so easily surmounted. The Building Committee, comprising some of the leading architects and engineers of the kingdom, among whom are Mr. Barry, the architect of the new Houses of Parliament, and Mr, Stephenson, the constructor of the Britannia Tubular Bridge, advertised for plans to be presented for the building. When the committee met, they found no want of designs ; their table was loaded with them, to the number of 249. Their first task was to select ihose which were positively worthless, and throw them aside. By ; this process the number for consideration was reduced to about sixty ; and from those the committee proceeded to concoct a design, w hich pleased nobody þÿ themselves least of all. However, the plan, such as it was, was decided upon, and advertisements were issued for tenders for its construction. This was the signal for a fierce onslaught upon the proceedings of the committee. For the erection of a building which was to be used for only a few months, more

more materials were to be thrown into , one of the main lungs of the metropolis, j than were contained in the eternal pyramid- of Egypt. Moreover, could the requisite number of miles of brickwork be constructed within the few weeks of time allotted? and was it not impossible that this should, in so short a time, be- I come sufficiently consolidated to sustain the weight of the immense iron dome which, according to the design of the committee, was to rest upon it 1 The committee, fortunately, were not compelled to answer these and a multitude of similar puzzling interrogatories which were poured in upon them. Relief was coining to them from an unexpected quarter: whence, we must go i back a little to explain. On New Year's Day, of the year 1839. Sir Robert Schomburgk, the botanist, was proceeding in a native boat up the River Berhice, in Betnerara. In a sheltered reach of the stream, he discovered resting upon the still waters an aquatic plant, a species of lily, but of a gigantic size, and of a shape hitherto unknow n, Seeds of this plant, to which was given the name of þÿ Victoria þÿRegia, were transmitted to England, and were ultimately committed to the charge of Joseph Paxton, the horticulturist at Chatsworlh, the magnificent seat of the Duke of Devonshire. The plant produced from these seeds became the occasion, and in certain respects the model, for the Crystal Palace.

IS very means were adopted to the plant in its accustomed circumstances. A tropical soil was formed for it of burned loam and peat; Newcastle coal was substituted for a meridian sun, i Illustration. t > produce an artificial South America under an English heaven ; by means of a wheel, a ripple like that of its native river, was communicated to the waters of the tank upon which its broad leaves reposed. This was not altogether a new task for Mr. Paxton, who had already devoted much attention to the erection of jjrecuhouses; and within the required space of time, he Imd completed this house for the þÿ Victoria þÿRegia, and therein, in the sense in which the acorn includes the oak, that of the Crystal Palace. While Mr. Paxton was planning an abode tor this Brobdignagian !d\. the B adding Committee ol the Exhibition were poring wearily over the þÿ 1) plans lying upon their table. They had rejected the 18 t worthless ones, and from the remainder had concocted, as we have said, with much cogitation ami I'-ttle satisfaction, their own design. þÿ Such as it was, however, it was d ternimed that it should he executed þÿ if possible. The building consists of three series of elevations of the respective heights of 64, 44, and 44 feet, intersected at the centre by a transept of 72 feet in width, having semicircular roof rising the a to height of 108 feet in the centre. It exlily could not do otherwise than flourish ; tends in length Idol feet from north to pleasure. In order to subdue the insouth, more than one-third of a mile, with a breadth of 45(! þÿl eetupon the ground; covering Id superficial acres, nearly double the extent of our own Washingtou-square ; and exceeding by more than one half the dimensions of the Park or the Battery. The whole rests upor. cast-iron pillars, united by bolts and nuts, fixed to flanges turned perfectly true, so that if the socket he placed level, the columns and connecting-pieces must stand upright ; and, in point of fact, not a crooked line is discoverable in the combination of such an immense number of pieces. For the support of the columns, holes are dug in the ground, in which is placed a bed of concrete, and upon this rest iron sockets of from three to four feet in J length, according to the level of the ground, to which the columns are (irmly attached by bolts and nuts. At the top, eaeii column is attached by a girder to its opposite column, both longitudinally and transversely, so that the whole eighteen acres of pillars is securely

The þÿroot s, of which there arc five, j one to each of the elevations, are constructed on the þÿ ridge and furrow principle, and glazed with sheets of glass of 41) inches in length. The construction will be at once understood by imagining a series of parallel rows of the letter \ (thus \ \ V), extending in uninterrupted lines the whole length of the building. þÿ Pile apex of each ridge is formed by a wooden sash-bar with notches upon each side for holding ihc laths in which are fitted the edges of the glass. The bottom bar, or rafter, is hollowed at the top so as to form a gutter to carry off the water, which passes through transverse gutters into the iron columns, which arc hollow, thus serving as waterpipes ; in the base of the columns horizontal pipes are inserted, which convey the accumulated water into the sewers. they had calculated the amount and cost The exhalations, from so large an extent of surface, from the plants, and from the breath of the innumerable visitors, rising and condensed against the glass, would descend from a flat roof in the form of a perpetual mist, but it is found that from glass pitched at a particular angle the moisture does not fall, but glides down its surface. The bottom bars are therefore grooved on the inside, thus forming interior gutters, by which the moisture also finds its way down the interior of the columns, þÿimprovement upon that through the drainage pipes, into the sewers. These grooved rafters, ofwhich the total length is 205 miles, are formed
by machinery, at a single operation.

The lower tier of the building is boarded, the walls of the upper portion being composed, like the roof, of glass. Ventilation is provided for by the basement portion being walled with iron plates, placed an angle of 45 degrees, known at as luffir-boarding , which admits the air freely, while it excludes the rain. A similar provision is made at the top of each tier of the building. These are so constructed that they can be closed at

tense light in a building having such an extent of glass surface, the whole roof and the south side will he covered with canvass, which will also preclude the possibility of in jury from hail, as w-ell as render the edifice much cooler. In the construction of the building care has been taken to give to each part the stillest and strongest form possible in a given quantity of material. The columns are hollow, and the girders which unite them are trellis-formed. þÿ The utmost weight which any girder w ill ever he likely to sustain in seven and a half tons ; and not one is used until after having been tested to the extent of 15 tons ; while the breaking weight is calculated at 30 tons. At first sight, there would seem to he danger that a building presenting so great a surface to the action of the wind, would bo liable to he blown down. But from the manner in which the columns are framed together they can not he overthrown except by breaking them. Experiments show that in order to break tiie 1060 columns on the ground floor, a force of 6360 tons must he exerted, at a height of 24 lcet. The greatest force of the w ind ever known is computed at 22 pounds to the superficial foot ; assuming a possible force of 28 pounds, and suppose a hurricane of that momentum to strike at once the whole side of the building, the total force would be less than 1500 tons þÿ not one-fourth of the capacity of the building to sustain, independent of the bracings, which add materially to its strength. So that, if

any reliance at all can be placed upon theoretical engineering, there can be no doubt as to the safety of the building. Entering at the main east or west entrance, we find ourselves in a nave 64 feet in height, 72 in breadth, and extending without interruption the whole length of the building, onc-third of a mile. Parallel with this, but interrupted by the transept in the centre, are a series of side aisles of 48 and 24 feet in breadth, with a height of 44 and 24 feet. Over the centre of the nave swells the semicircular roof of the transept, overarching the stately trees beneath þÿ a Brobdignagian green-house with ancient elms instead of geraniums and rosebushes. The whole area of the ground lloor is 772,784 square feet ; and that of the galleries 217,100; making in all within a fraction of one million square feet ; to which may be added 500,000 feet of hanging-space, available for the display of the products of human heads and hands. There arc three refreshment rooms, one in the transept, and one near each

end, around the trees which were left standing, where ices and pastry for the wealthy, and bread-and-butter and cheese for the poorer are to be furnished. No wine, spirits, or fermented liquors are to be sold ; only tea, coffee, and unfermented drinks ; pure water is to be furnished gratis to all comers by the lessees of the refreshment rooms. In respect to the decoration of the interior, a keen controversy has been waged. The fact of iron being the material of construction renders it necessary that it should be painted to preserve it from the action of the atmosphere. On the one hand, it is said that the fact that the structure is metallic should be indicated by the decoration, otherwise the whole will have no more appearance of stability than an arbor of j wickerwork. Those who take this view recommend that the interior should be bronzed. On the other hand, those to whom the decoration is intrusted affirm that the object of using color is to increase the effect of light and shade. If the whole were of one uniform dead of which the building is composed, all color the effect of the innumerable parts J falling in similar lines, one before the other, would he precisely that of a plane j surface ; the extended lines of pillars presenting the aspect of a continuous wall. In order to bring out the distinctive features of the building various colors must be used ; and experiments 1 show that a combination of the primary colors, red, blue, and yellow, is most pleasant to the eye. The best means

for using these is to place blue, which retreats, upon the concave surfaces, yellow, which advances, upon the convex ones, reserving red for plane surfaces. Hut as when these colors come in contact each become tinged with the complementary color of tin other þÿ the blue with green, the red with orange þÿ a line of white is interposed between them. Applying these principles, the shafts of the columns are to be yellow, the concave portions of their capitals blue, the under side of the girders red, and their vertical surfaces white. Among all the wonders of the Crystal Palace nothing is more wonderful than its cheapness, and the rapidity of its construction. Possession of the site was obtained on the 31)tli of July; in a period of only 145 working-days the building was to all intents and purposes completed. As to cheapness it costs less per cubic foot than an ordinary barn. If used only for the Exhibition, and at. its close returned to the contractors, the cost will be nine-sixteenths of a penny a foot; or, if permanently purchased, it will be one penny and onetwelfth. Thus: The solid contents are þÿ. 13, 000, (K)0 cubic feet ; the price if retimed is £79,800, if retained £150,000. This simple fact, that a building of glass and iron, covering eighteen acres, affording room for nine miles of tables, should have been completed in less than five months from the day when the contract was entered into, at a cost less than that of the humblest hovel, opens a new era in the science of building.

Alter being (within a few hours) six days overdue, the steamer, with the 2nd March mails, arrived on Sunday. The ministerial crisis has been so far overcome that Lord John Russell and his colleagues had consented to resume oflice, but whether they w ill he aide to carry on the government w ith anything like public advantage, or individual satisfaction, appears more than ever doubtful front the powerful and every day increasing opposition of their policy. þÿ The objectionable Budget of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and the Anti- Papal Aggression Bill of the Premier, formidable obstructions of themselves, are not the only stumbling blocks in the political course of the present administration. Lord John Russell would do well to look into the Colonial Office, and see whether- that department had not fully contributed to hasten the recent crisis in which his government was placed, and whether it be not still possessed of the ingredients to aid in bringing about a similar result. It is no part of the duty of the Colonial Office to be the apologist of delinquent or tyrannical Governors. In all cases of complaint against such officials, it should decide impartially and faithfully, and irrespective of the position of the parties. Were such a line of conduct observed, Her Majesty's Colonial subjects would be relieved of much cause of disappointment, and a better system of government would be established. It is only necessary v to refer to the tyrannical J and san-

guinary conduct of Lord Torrington, in Ceylon, justify this conclusion. It is, to indeed, our lirm conviction, arrived at after deliberate consideration of the qin stion, that Lord John Russell could not possibly perform an act more calculated to endear him to llcr Majesty's Colonial subjects than by delegating to tin in the privilege of periodically, say every lour or live years, electing their own President, who should be invested with all the rights and privileges at present enjoy' d by the Executive sent from England. þÿ The " signs of the times1' indicate that such will be the case before long, and his lordship may as well aid and anticipate the " good time coming." The principle of self-government is fast gaining ground in public opinion. Sir \V. Molesworth, in the House of Commons, on the 3rd ultimo, bad given notice of two resolutions which he intended to move on the subject, on the 13th instant. The 1st, þÿ " That it is the opinion of this House that steps should be taken to relieve this country as speedily as possible from its present civil and military expenditure on account of those colonics w hich are neither military stations nor convict settlements. 2nd, þÿ That it is expedient at the same time to give the inhabitants of those colonies ample powers for their local self-government, and to free them from that imperial interference with their allairs w hich is inseparable from

tlieir present military occupation." þÿ There was no House on the 13th, nor do we perceive any notice of these resolutions on the following day, but there can he no doubt that Sir \\ illiam will take an early day to bring them forward. We shall look with much interest for the result, and sincerely hope the principle will be conceded. It is perpetually said that the cost of the Colonies is against this proposal are to be considergreater than their worth to Great Britain. This surely, should lie an argument in favor of sell-government, and should Sir W. Molesworth's motion he even more with a view to relieve Great Britain of tilis cost than to benefit the Colonies by soil-government, we shall still be thank- Jill to him þÿ for so persuaded are we that the measure will he a benefit to the Cololues. that we care not by what means it he ell'eeted, so long as it is effected. þÿ But what will the Colonies do without the military, will, no doubt, be the exclamation of the nervous and fearful of the inhabitants? We answer, substitute an efficient police in their place, who will be sufficient to keep the peace of the country. We should he sorry to see the troops removed, as they are the means of throwing into circulation a large amount of money per annum, but i: self-government cannot be conceded without their being removed, we say remove them by all means. - " d CV"

I must state it to be my conviction, that the glorious times we have passed through, and in which llic ttniJy, fidelity, mid loir of country, animating our people, have been proved by deeds never to be forgotten, our Country has become remarkable by the phenomenon of the elasticity of the people, and its capacily of labour, by which it has been able to bear heavy taxes, occasioned by the war, and nevertheless procure labour enough to sustain the productivity of our land, which, after three years war, is as active as ever. such circumstances, this will in future time, stand as a remarkable example of what the Danish People may do. þÿ [Meeting of 3d February.

AI»ICIL 1801. To Young Men. There is no moral object so beautiful to me as the conscientious young man. I watch him as I do a star in the heavens ; clouds may be before him, but we know that his light is behind them, arid will beam again ; the blaze of þÿothers popularity may outshine him, hut we know that though unseen, lie illuminates his own true sphere. lie resists temptation not without a struggle, for that is not a virtue, but he does resist and conquer; he bears the sarcasms of the profligate, and it stings him, for that is the trial of virtue, but lie heals the wound with his own pure touch. He heeds not the watchword of fashion, if it leads to sin ; the atheist, who says not only in his heart, but with his lips, þÿ There is no þÿGod, controls him not ; he sees the hand of a creating God, and rejoices in it. Woman is sheltered by fond arms and loving counsel ; old age is protected by experience, and manhood by its strength ; hut the young man stands amid the temptations of the world, like a self-balanced power ; happy is he who seeks and gains the prop and shelter of morality. Onward, then, conscientious youth ! raise thy standard and nerve thyself for

lectual power, awaken it in that cause ; let it not he said of thee, he helped to swell the tide of sin by pouring his influence into its channels. If thou art feeble in mental strength, throw not that drop m a polluted current. Awake, arise, young man ! assume the beautiful garb of virtue ! It is fearfully easy to sin ; it isdifficult to be pure and holy. Rut on thy strength then ! let Truth be the lady of thy love þÿ defend her.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis! Mr. Editor, Some time in last month, at a public meeting of inhabitants of this town and others, a committee was elected, that was to take into consideration matters of importance connected with the general welfare of the island. The subject deemed to be of first importance was the petitioning for Compensation for emancipated slaves. This motion animated many hearts, but particularly the hearts of former owners of non-predial slaves, as it held out to them the expectation, or raised their hopes of success, (this being the most favorable period to start the subject) in being rewarded for the great loss sustained by the Emancipation. The excitement caused by these suggestions has not abated ; fur 1 am , and I feel persuaded that every person concerned is anxiously waiting to hear the results ot the þÿCommittee conference. s We have been waiting long ; and hope that we shall not be disappointed. We trust that the matter was not of an cphemeric nature ; but that our sanguinary anticipations will be realized in shortly seeing a notice in your columns, inviting us to come together again, in order to hear the noble appeal, and, to which we trust, we shall all be able to respond most heartily þÿ Amen. I am, dear Sir, An Inhabitant. Christiansted April 14th, 1851. ««< Mr. Editor þÿ I beg you will give the following remarks a place in your Paper : þÿ Our gracious Sovereign having granted a liberal Constitution to his subjects in Denmark, we his equally loyal sub-

jects in the danish westindia Islands, are naturally anxious to participate in its promised advantages. We are emboldened to hope that our just wishes will find favour with our wise and good King, as he has most graciously declared in his letter patent to us, of the 22nd September 1848, þÿ That he encircles all the inhabitants of his Westindia Islands with equal paternal þÿaffection. The Honorable Members of the li u rgher Council of this Island, arc especially called on to advocate the legal rights of their Constituents (who are inhabitants of the Island, without any invidious distinctions) praying bis Majesty, that the rich gilt bestowed on our fellow Subjects in the Mother Country, may also be extended to their brothers in the West, whose hearts are þÿDenmark s. The groveling and sordid views of a few men, who, aiming at power and sclfintcrest, would willingly sacrifice, not only their own just rights, but also the sacred prerogatives of their fellow citizens, to obtain their selfish ends, ought not to influence the minds of the worthy and chosen representatives ofthc people. The intellectual inhabitants of the lanish westindia islands cannot be expected to remain supine and indifferent to their true interests, in this eventful era, when nearly the whole human fami-

st, <s » © )i t£ A T tl 3. ly (including even the unmtellectual portion) are striving to obtain their political rights. The humble petitions of our Northern Profilers fora Constitution, having been most graciously acceded to by our beloved King ; the sacred duty devolves on us, to endeavour to secure the same blessing for ourselves and children. This can only be obtained by convening public meetings þÿ making known our grievances by exercising the legal right
ges may be graciously accorded us by our brave and beloved Monarch. Your obdt. servt. U. P. St. Croix, 8th April 1851.

Bruno Bauer, the Coryphaeus of German Rationalism (unless Strauss may be thought to be a rival for that questionable eminence) whose last work is devoted to the somewhat useless task of proving, with a superabundance of logic and contemptuous irony, that the late Frankfort Parliament effected nothing, and knew nothing, has run through a singular career. He was born in 1809, and in his twentieth year commenced the study of theology at Berlin. Five years later he became private teacher in the University, at which time he belonged to Hegelian school of orthodoxy. The germ of his subsequent views, however, may be found in his þÿ Kritik of the Old Testament þÿWritings, in which he represents þÿ the myths of Judaism in their successive transformations, as a development of the national sentiment of the þÿJews. He first fairly broke ground with orthodoxy in 1839, when he began to apply his principles of criticism to the New Testament narratives. He commenced with the Gospel of John, which he regarded as a work of the imagination, with but here and there a historical trace þÿ a work merely þÿ founded upon þÿfacts. He had, meanwhile, been transferred to the University of Bonn, where he proceeded with his three volumes of criticisms upon the other Evangelists, at the conclusion of which he found he had reached a point which lie could hardly have anticipated at the outset. In the first volume he had begged that the judgment of his readers might he suspended ; þÿ for however bold and far-reaching the negations

of this volume might appear, it would be manifest that the most searching criticism would most fully set forth the reative power of Jesus and of his prinþÿciples; and even in the second volume he seems to allow to the main facts set forth in the life of Jesus a historical verity ; but at the conclusion of the work he makes it doubtful whether such a person as Jesus ever existed. Bauer now occupied the anomalous position of a theological teacher who represented the Gospels to be mere works of the imagination, possessing no higher historical value than þÿXenophon Cyropaedia, s or þÿFenelon Telemachus, s characterized Matthew and Luke as stupid copyists of Mark, denounced theologians as hypocrites, and the science of theology as the dark stain upon modern history. It is no wonder that the Prussian Minister of Worship felt himself impelled to inquire of the Theological Faculty, what was the position of Bauer in relation to Christianity, and whether he should be allowed to exercise his functions. The Faculty were embarrassed : on the one hand, they feared that freedom of inquiry would be trenched upon were he silenced; and on the other, that the cause of religion would be injured were he allowed to teach. Finally, a middle course was adopted, and he was allowed to teach in the philosophical faculty;

þÿ o<X> «þÿ ON SIX. Sin is called mortal or deadly, because it brings death to the soul. There are three sorts of death, which are the consequence and effect of sin ; a spiritual death, a temporal death, an eternal death. A spiritual death consists in the privation of grace, and all its concomitant blessings. A temporal death consists in the miseries and afflictions of this life, and particularly in the last instant, which shall put an end to it. Eternal death consists in the damnation of the soul, after its departure from the body. Three dreadful punishments of which sin is the unhappy cause. Spiritual death is a privation of grace, and ol all the attendants of grace: because this death does not work its dreadful effects perceptibly to the sinner, it will perhaps appear less terrible to lum : but alas ! with what mortal wounds

I is his soul pierced through, and to what a woful situation is it reduced? Being dead in the eyes of God, and deprived of the life of grace, it is stripped of its possessions, it is degraded from its dignities, it is forsaken by God, and given up a prey to the gnawing worm, which tears it in pieces. My God, what miseries are these ! Temporal death, which is another punishment of sin, comprises all melancholy events, doleful accidents, unfortunate changes, tragical ends, and innumerable other misfortunes; for in vain do we look for any other cause of these disasters than sin, which is the most common source of them. In effect, was it not sin, which, from the earliest times, brought down the destructive deluge upon the earth? Was it not sin which drew tire from heaven on the polluted towns of Sodom and Gomorrah, and their criminal inhabitants ? Did not sin arm the hand of the destroying angel against the first-born of Egypt ? Was it not sin that called forth llery serpents in the desert ? Was it not sin which opened the earth to swallow down the wicked Dathan and Abiron ? And without having recourse to these distant examples, from whence proceed so many other disasters with which the world is, as it were, overwhelmed ? From whence so many unforeseen and melancholy accidents? And can any one be so wilfully blind as not to see in all this the visible vengeance of God, and acknow ledge the just punishment of sin? But alas ! are these great, these terrible truths, to many of those, w ho arc

now reading or hearing them, only simple threats? How many of these persons are perhaps destined to a speedy death ! How many to a sudden death ? How many will perhaps conclude their days amidst the extravagances of a wild presumption, or in a woful, and voluntary impenitence, or in a still more deplorable despair ? What a lot? what misery ? Vet we stand unconcerned, wTe remain thoughtless of it ; whilst perhaps at this very moment the dreadful decree is passing against us ? perhaps God has already cut us off, and destined us to punishment; perhaps in a little time he will command the stroke to be struck ; and we are still running after the amusements and foolish pleasures ofthe world, and live peaceably in sin. Is our conduct folly, is it blindness, or is it a renunciation of our faith?

No man had better opportunity lieu Fielding to he acquainted with the statr ol the poor ; let us listen to him. þÿ That the poor are a very great burden, and even a nuisance to the kingdom ; that the laws for relieving their distresses i and restraining their vices, have not an swered ; and that they are at present 13 21 / very ill provided for and much worse governed, are truths which every one will acknowledge. Every person who I hath property, must feel the weight of the tax that is levied lor the poor ; and every person of understanding, must see how absurdly it is applied. So useless indeed is this heavy tax, and so wretched its disposition, that it is a question, whether the poor or rich are actually more dissatisfied ; since the plunder ol tiiv one serves so little to the real advantage of the other; for while a million yearly is raised among the rich, many ot the poor are starved; many more languish in want and misery; of the resi, numbers tire found begging or pilferinsr in the streets to-day, and to-morrow are locked up in gaols and Bridewells. If wc were to make a progress through the outskirts of the metropolis and look into the habitations of the poor, we should there behold such pictures of human misery, as must move the compassion of every heart that deserves the name of human. What indeed must ho hicomposition, who could see whole families in want of every necessary of life, oppressed with hunger, cold, nakedness, and tilth ; and with diseases, the certain

consequence of all these ! 'i lie suff erings indeed of the poor are less known than their misdeeds ; and therefore we are less apt to pity them. They starve, and freeze, and rot, among themselves ; but they beg, and steal, and rob, among their þÿbetters.

It was with feelings of astonishment, bordering on disgust, that I read in your last paper, the notice of the rationalist Bruno Bauer. Such men in my opinion could bt more appropriately stiled irrationalists , for I cannot consider that man sane, who utters such blasphemies against the inspired or God-breathed Word and who doubts of the existence of our Lord. I do not praise your taste for inserting such examples of human depravity þÿ and I think you would do better to edify, than disgust your subscribers ; for although such a notice may in some degree, by showing the depths to which the darkened understanding of a depraved will may descend, warn others, yet I think the columns of your paper could be more usefully occupied. I remain, Dear Sir, Your obedt. Servt, A. N. 20th April 1851.

MR. niCItllADV. (From the þÿ Athenaeum.") On Wednesday last, Mr. Macready took his final farewell of the stage. This important theatrical event occurred within the walls of old Drury, and on the boards which Mr. Macready, during his management, sought to raise to respectability and distinction. The tragedy selected for the occasion was þÿ Macþÿbeth. The noble Thane was, of course, supported by Mr. Macready himself þÿ Macduff being undertaken by Mr. Phelps, best and Lady Macbeth by Mrs. Warner. On the manner in which these respective parts were sustained the occasion does not demand that we should be critical þÿ suffice it to record that no nervousness or want of self-possession marred the efforts of either. Yet, the audience was most multitudinous and enthusiastic. It had been necessary to guard the entrances to the theatre by police, who made a passage for the playgoer through the excited crowd in the streets. Within the theatre, the orchestra was converted I into stalls, and the number of persons admitted into the pit and gallery was judiciously limited. Owing to these arrangements, notwithstanding the general enthusiasm, order was maintained, and the requisite silence attended the deeper portions of the tragic scene. At the conclusion, Mr. Macready came before the curtain in a suite of black, to deliver his farewell address. It was long before the impassioned burst which greeted this last appearance of the actor on the scene of many a former triumph would permit a hearing to what he came

to say. The audience appeared as if willing to defer the final parting ; and Mr. Macready, during this last and lingering grasp, as it were, of the public hand, seemed in danger of losing the self-possession necessary to carry him through

roar of the house subsided into silence þÿ and out of its stillness arose, often faltering with emotion, the one voice, to deliver the following address : þÿ þÿ last theatrical My part is played ; and, in accordance with long-established usage, I appear once more before you. Even if I were without precedent for the discharge of this act of duty, it is one which my own feelings would irresistibly urge upon me ; for, as I look back on my long professional career, 1 see in it but one continuous record of indulgence and support extended to me, 1 cheering me in my onward progress, and upholding me in most trying emergencies. J have, therefore, been desirous of offering you my parting acknowledgments for the partial kindness with which my humble efforts have uniformly been received, and for a life made happier by your favour. The distance of five and thirty years has not dimmed my recollection of the encouragement which gave fresh impulse to the inexperienced essays of my youth, and stimulated me to perseverance when struggling hardly for equality of position with the genius and talent of those artists whose superior excellence I un-

3 <0 m <Q a ATIS, , grudgingly admitted, admired and honoured. That encouragement helped to place me, in respect to privileges and emolument, on a footing with my distinguished competitors. With the growth of time, your favour seemed to grow: and, undisturbed in my hold upon your opinion, from year to year I found friends more closely and around me. All I can advance to testify how justly 1 have appreciated the patronage thus liberally awarded me, is the devotion throughout those years of my energies your to service. My ambition to establish a theatre, in regard to decorum and taste worthy of our country, and to leave in it the plays of our divine Shakspeare, fully illustrated, was frustrated by those whose was, in virtue of the trust committed to them, themselves to have undertaken the task. But some good seed has yet been sown ; and, in the zeal and creditaide productions of certain of our present managers, we have assurance that the corrupt editions and unseemly presentations of past days will never be restored, but that the purity of our great þÿpoet t s ext will henceforward be held on our English stage in the reverence it ever should command. I have little more to say. By some, the relation of an actor to his audience is considered slight and transient. 1 do not feel so. þÿ The repeated manifestation, under circumstances personally affecting me, of jour favourable sentiments towards me, will live with life among my most grate- 1 u 1 memories ; and, because I would not willingly abate one jot in your esteem,

We believe Mr. Gordon to have been the first engineer to introduce east iron for this useful purpose ; the advantages of which, in point of economy, durability, and rapidity of execution, are unquestionable. Seen at a short distance from the abovementioned works, it forms a handsome column of good proportions, the lantern ami gallery at top giving a complete fun h to the design. The figure of the column is conoidnl, its lower external diameter living I feet <> inches, and that of the top part under the gnliery, 10 feet 10 inches. The lower (Hates are I inch thick, while those of the upper part of the column are reduced to s ol an inch thickness. the lower plates; in these cases the llanges are i! inches in width. The external door, which is also of Last India teak wook, and 3 inches thick, is hung with hinges of gun metal, and is furnished wit Ii a stout lock anil other fastenings. in the centre of the column is a vertical hollow cylinder, to he used as a channel for the weight of the revolving

raising and lowering provisions, stores, &.c. Arrival of the Tkizi Baari, with Turkish Contributions. þÿ Tlie Turkish frigate Teizi Baari, arrived at Southampton on Saturday, from Constantinople, having left that port on the 6th inst. She has on hoard 207 packages, containing, 3,000 articles for the Great Exhibition. The articles consist of silk and gold embroidered fabrics, dresses, silks, and cloaks, from Brussa, Albania, and other places in Turkey, celebrated for such manufactures, splendid specimens of fire-arms, carpets, and shawls, a large quantity of beautiful and interesting specimens of the natural productions of Turkey, consisting of roots, leaves, and flowers. There is also on board a carriage sledge, magnificently ornamented and inlaid with gold, and a caique, in charge of Turkish rowers, who will exhibit their skill and the swiftness of their boat on the Serpentine. Amongst the distinguished persons who have arrived in the Teizi Baari are, Gemeledin Pacha, a near relative of the Sultan of Turkey, on a visit to this country during the Exhibition ; Vice-Admiral Mustupha Pacha, an oificer of the highest rank in the Ottoman dominions ; M. Constantino Mussurus, the new ambassador from the Sublime Porte to the Court of St. James's. In addition to these most distinguished persons, there are a large number of Turkish noblemen and gentlemen. The Teizi Baari is a war steamer lbout 1,800 tons burden and 4.50 horse power. Iler armament consists of 12 heavy brass guns and two swivels ; she is Turkish built ; her officers and crew

consist of about 350 persons. Two or three of her engineer officers are Englishmen. As soon as she arrived, the Ottoman llag was hoisted on board the of the town. A naval officer in uniform ships in the harbour, and various parts the proceeded from the Admiralty Otlicc to with pay his respects on hoard as the representative of the British Government. This officer took charge of and brought ashore despatches from the British embnssv at Constantinople to Lord Palmerston which had been sent by the Teizi Baari. It being contrary to civic etiquette for the Mayor of Southampton to c tro on board the Ottoman frigate o before lie bad received a visit from the chief persons in command of her, bis worship, as soon as the frigate had been board for bis kindness. They were t hen saluted by the town, deputed three gentlemen, Mr. Deacon, town-clerk, Mr. vStebbing, Town Councillor, and Mr. Cooper, connected with one of the public departments in the town, to go oft' to the steamer and offer the services at his command to facilitate the communications of the distinguished persons on board with the shore or town. The deputation from the mayor having arrived alongside the steamer, sent up their cards to an officer, and were admitted on board. Turkish marines on guard in red coats were pacing about on the paddle-boxes. The deck appeared < rowded with sailors, marines, officers, and passengers, many of the latter dres-

þÿ þÿ - <0 'Ji (D 1 ATI 3-. sed picturesquely. The great majority of the countenances appeared Turkish. Amongst the sailors, however, therewere some Abyssinian faces. In a few minutes a dragoman appeared on deck and, having ascertained the object of tiie deputation, tile gentlemen forming the latter were ushered with great respect below and into the saloon. This was earpetted and the iittings-up and furniture were remarkably elegant. The gentlemen were introduced by the dragoman to the ambassador, M. Mussurus, who appeared lo be about forty years of age, with an intelligent Greek countenance, and a very pleasing and vivacious address. Genieledin Pacha a kins-'man of the Ottoman Sultan, soon entered the saloon, lie is about thirty-live years of age, and one of the handsomest men in Turkey. Both t lie ambassador and Getneledin Pacha wore military frock coats and the Turkish fez. The gentlemen were invited to sit on chairs, and in a few moments servants entered with splendid oriental calumets of immense length, filled with lighted Turki. h tobacco. Each gentleman was presented with one. Bound each tube was a ring of precious stones; the bowl rested on the carpet, the mouthpieces were of aiuber, too large to be admitted into the mouth, the lips therefore merely surrounded the orifice from which the delicious vapour of I lie weed was drawn up. The absence of Vice-Admiral Muslaplia Pacha from the saloon was apohtgised for, on the ground of fatigue, lie was afterwards seen. He is a diminu-

tive man, very plainly dressed between forty and fifty years of age. He speaks English pretty well. While enjoying the calumet in the saloon, M. Mussurus entered into an animated conversation with the town clerk on our municipal institutions. Gcuielediu Pacha spoke of Exhibition, and seemed surprised when informed of the splendid ceremony which it was designed that the þÿ Great Exliib turn s.iould be inaugurated. He inquired as to the etiquette of visiting the mayor, and very willingly consented to comply with it in paying the first visit. On the departure of the deputation, Gemelcdin Pacha begged their acceptance of ii present, according to the eastern custom, and they were requested to convey to the mayor of May S. American Southampton the thanks of those on

escorted to the gangway by Captain Shauisi Bey and the officers of the ship, and After a visit lias been paid to the mayor by the Turks, the mayor will return the visit in state, escorted by the officers of the corporation, in their official robes, and accompanied by the regalia of the corporation, the symbols of bis rank as chief magistrate of the town and admiral of the port, when an address will be delivered to the vice-admiral, welcoming him and his distinguished companions to Southampton, and expressive of the respect and veneration for the many virtues of t lie Turkish character and nation. Every effort will be made to get out the goods for the Exhibition from the frigate on Monday,

The frost that nips the opening bloom, The blight that seals the flow' ret' s doom, The famine's hungry, spectre form, The spotted plague and sweeping storm, The quicksand' s deep cngidphing snare, The sunken rock that baffles care, The adder's foul and fatal sting, The panther's sudden, deadly spring, The robber's grasp and rifling hand, The cloaked assassin's ruthless brand. These fearful things colled in one, And yet you'll find them all outdone fflol by a \ flood's wide-sweeping tide, Or fields where death and carnage ride : fflot by the lightning's scathing flash, Or by the earthquake's whelming crash ; But by the stand' rer's pest-like breath, That smites your name with worse than death ; That, charged with poison straight from hell, Begets all things than plagues more fell ; That often dims young genius' rye, That severs Friendship's fondest tie; And often too has darkly spread A cloud around fair I irtue's head. Apprenticeship is the most important stage of Jifo through which a mechanic is called to pass ; it is emphatically the spring season ot his flays þÿ the time when he is sowing the seed, the Iruits ot which he is to reap in after years. If he spare no labour in its proper culture, he is sure of obtaining an abundant harvest ; but if. in the culture of the mental soil, he follows the example of many in tilling the earth, and carelessly and negli- ill gently does his work, like them, he v find the seeding time past, and his ! ground only bringing forth weeds and briars, Let the young apprentice hear 111 mind, when lie commences learning ,u y business, that all hopes of success in the future are doomed to fade away like the morning mist, unless he improve the golden season. I.et him bear in mind that he can become master o( his business only through the closest application and the most persevering industry, and that unless he docs master it he may hid farewell to all the visions of future prospects and success. The apprenticeship is the foundation of the if great mechanical edifice ; and surely the foundation of a structure he not firm, the structure itself crumbles and falls to the earth. Apprentices ! persevere ; he studious and attentive ; the road to honour and distinction is equally open to all ; study well all the branches of your business, both practical and theoretical þÿ and you will not tail, when the time shall come, to take an active part in life, to he of use, not only in

From the St. Thomas Times, May 24. We publish to-day the interesting particulars of the opening of a steam packet route between England and Denmark. The Danish Authorities, aware of the great importance of a speedy and independent communication between the two Countries, have contributed their utmost to render practicable the operations ot the Steam Packet Company, who, in conjunction with the Eastern Counties Railway, have undertaken to convey passengers between Lowestoft, in Suffolk, and the seaport of Hjerting, in Jutland, at a cost so small, and a speed so great, as to put rivalry out of the question. Hjerting and Lowestoft arc the natural termini of any chain of connexion between the Danish and the British metropolis; and trial trips have recently been made in the Royal Mail Steamer Prince, Captain Hart, in order to test the practicability of the route. þÿ The reception at Copenhagen of the representatives of the London press who accompanied the party was very courteous. On their arrival they were introduced to Count Sponneck, the Minister of Finance, who expressed his I while there every prospect gratification at the opening of the line of communication, and assured them that every means should be taken to render the travelling as expeditious as possible. His Excellency gave the gentlemen an introduction to the Castle of Frcdcricksborg, the magnificent residence of llis Majesty the King, situate about 20 miles north of the capital, of which the party availed themselves the following day. They were received by

the Lord Chamberlain Berling, and after passing a few most agreeable hours with him, discussing the merits of the ; gen, via England, in the short space of various routes, His Majesty (having heard of the arrival of the party in his dominions) was graciously pleased to honour them with an interview. His Majesty appears to take a deep personal interest in the new enterprise individu-

from its being calculated to draw his dominions in close proximity to England, to which it gives a separate and distinct means of sending mails, an advantage that, in case of war, would be of very palpable importance, llis Majesty was extremely affable throughout the interview, during which he expressed his thanks to the English press for the zeal,
maintenance of the interests and honour of the Danish Crown against its revolted

the interview we are describing, llis Majesty conversed in French, making such inquiries relative to the particulars of the journey as showed him to be thoroughly conversant with the entire scope of the expedition in its objects and details, llis Majesty was dressed in a plain dark green military frock coat, and had a small hanger-shaped weapon, rather less than a foot in length, suspended from his girdle. W e are glad to find that the impertinence and austerity so frequently displayed in these distant parts, by the generality of the Subordinates in the employment of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, have only to be represented, to be corrected ; and we hope that no case of vexatious and wanton inconvenience will in any instance be permitted to pass unrepresented, and unredressed. To the Secretary of the Royal M ail Steam Packet Company, Moor gate Street, London.

Antigua, Deer. 14th 1850. Sir, þÿ Permit me through the medium of yourself to draw the attention of the Acting Committee of the R. M. S. P. Company to the following grievance which I am induced to lay before their Hoard having been advised so to do by several influential Gentlemen of this Island. Having to go to the Island of St. Thomas on particular business, 1 proposed going as a Deck Passenger on hoard the Steamer þÿ þÿEagle which was due here on the Morning of the 15th I\ovr. Accordingly 1 went to English Harbor for the purpose and was in the Dock Yard when the þÿpassenger s boat came to the wharf, 1 presented myself to the Purser and informed him that it wis my intention to take a passage to St. Thomas on board the Steamer. My trunk was put in the boat, and the Purser enquired if I was a Cabin or Deck Passenger, and on my stating that I was the latter, he positively refused my entering the boat as such. 1 informed him that it was in accordance with their Rales to take Deck Passengers intercolonially ; this lie said he cared not about, and instantly had my trunk taken out of the boat. 1 was, therefore, disappointed in proceeding, and was put to a great deal of expense. I hope you will bring such conduct as this to notice, and thereby prevent a like occurrence. I remain, Sir, Your Old. Servt., JACOH Wm. FONSECA.

TERRIFIC STORY OF PIRACY AND MURDER (From the Port of Spain Gazette, 31a rch 14.)
Two sailors by the name of Reed ui.a Clements, have lately been executed in Richmond, Virginia, for the crime of piracy and murder, on the high seas þÿ

The Richmond Dispatch publishes the following letter from one of the accused, who is represented to he late a young and intelligent man : LETTER 1ROM REED, the PIRATE. Richmond, Va., July 1, 1850. l/ Pear Father, Mother , Brother and Sisters / It is with a heart full of grief and woe, and a trembling hand, that I take my pen o address you, I had a great mind of not letting you know for 1 know it will he heart rending news to you all. So, my dear parents, forgive me my past offences to you, as I hope God will have mercy on my soul for which I hope you will pray, dear parents. I am now confined in Richm'd county jail with another person and on no less a charge than mutiny and murder on the high seas. I will explain to you the whole affair. I was paid off from a U. S. sloop of war in December last. She was stationed in the Gulf of Mexico, and 1 was persuaded by my shipmate, Clements by name, to take a short trip to the West Indies. So I consented, knowing it would he but of two or three months, and at my return it would be a good time to cross the Atlantic, and view once more the scenes of my early days. Rut þÿGod will s must be done, and instead of returning back in joy, I was confined in jail to stand my trial on the first Monday in November next. E. Clements and myself shipped on board of a schooner in Elizabeth City, N. C., about 40 miles from Norfolk, where I was paid off, and proceeded to the West Indies. We touched at two or three different islands until we arrived at

Port of Spain, Island of Trinidad, where we discharged our cargo, and took a passenger on board, and proceeded to sea on the 27lh of January last. On that fatal night an affair took place, a few minutes after I relieved the passenger from the wheel. At 10 þÿo clockthe mate and passenger went forward to sway up the tore peak. This man, Clements, who belonged to the watch below, slept on deck this night, as he generally was in the habit of doing in lair weather in that hot climate. The mate aroused him up to sway up the fore peak of the foresail, but it being his watch below, he refused, and so a scuffle ensued. The mate took a piece of hand-spike and struck him several times ; but after the aflray was going on m fierce combat, I perceived that the. passenger had a dirk or knife in his hand, and was making towards Clements with an intent, J expect, of killing him. I then left the wheel and grasped the passenger by the wrist, thinking to take the knife from him, but he grabbled me by the thigh with one hand, and canted me on the rail of the schooner. I then thought I would he certainly thrown overboard, hut I twisted his dirk knife out of his hand, and to save myself I had to turn his own weapon on himself, when befell to rise no more, and saved me from a watery grave ; hut I fear for a worse one, as there was no witness to the affair. During this time Clements had killed the mate with his

ST, <B & <D at 31 ATI sheath knife. The Captain being in the cabin, heard an unusual noise on deck, and taking his pistols came on deck, and without asking what was the matter, fired at Clements and me twice in succession. We having a brace of pistols in the forecastle, we got them and determined to defend ourselves. The Captain, after firing returned to the cabin, where lie did not long remain, hut came on deck while I stood by the mainmast. The Captain, on seeing me fired the pistol at me, then fired unue and graz- l ed Ins throat slightly, hut 1 did not know he was wounded. I then re-loaded and went aft to the cabin door to let him know how all this sad affair occurred ; but before I could speak to him he fired at me, and slightly wounded me on the nose, which can scarcely be perceived I also fired my pistol hut it being dark, in the cabin, it dul no injury. So vve went forward and told the man that was in the forecastle (Costello) what had happened, and we then all three determined to defend ourselves in case the Captain should attack us. The vc el was close hauled on a wind without any' person at t lie helm. In this deplorable condition we remained for two days with little to eat or drink, when we hailed the Captain and asked him for the boat. þÿ April iksteds After some hesitation he said we could take it and leave the vessel, which we concluded would he the safest, so as not to spill any more blood on either side. þÿ After Clements and myself had got into the boat, this other man took an axe and ! at Estate Peters Best on the

cut the þÿboat painter. s We expected all the time that lie would go with us. So, we were left at the mercy of the seas, without chart, compass or quadrant. þÿ We had two oars and a sail. So immediately after making sail on the boat, we put her before the wind, the N. E. trade wind blowing in those latitudes. In two days we reached a small Island. We were almost famished with hunger and thirst. We travelled some of this island in quest of water, hut could not find any ; hut night coming on we returned to find our boat, hut missed our way and did not find her then. So, we laid down on the rocks almost in despair. About 12 þÿo clock I awoke þÿ the moon being high in the heavens. I found myself greatly refreshed, and we proceeded to look for the boat, but we did not so far before we fell in with two Spaniards. þÿ The first thing we asked for was a drink of water, and they gave us about a quart, which they had in a calabash, the first , we had since leaving the vessel. We then soon found the boat, and we went to the west end of the island where we found a hut with three Spaniards, the only inhabitants of the island, their only occupation being hunt ng wild cattle, which they captured by the lasso and traps. We remained there about five days, and after getting all the necessary information concerninthe Spanish Main, we started early one morning from our island and in two or three days we reached a place called Jgarta, where having no passport, our boat was seized by the commandant. We then paid our pas-

sage and went to East I.aguayra, where we were put in jail and kept there about three months when we were sent to Norfolk and examined, and afterwards committed to Richmond jail to stand our trial in November next.

" lie it known that it is our desire, whenever circumstances permit, to alleviate the burdens which the disturbances of the last year have brought upon our Duchy of Schleswig, and that, respecting the state of siege which has been proclaimed in the southern part of the Duchy and which we cannot, as yet, altogether abolish, we have resolved upon the immediate introduction ot such modifications as are warranted by the altered circumstances. We are informed that instructions have been forwarded by a gentleman of this town, to W. II. Shew, Esquire, Barrister at Law in Tortola, to file an action against the Stipendiary Justice and the Provost Marshal of that Island, for false imprisonment, ft would appear from the intelligence which has reached our office, that in the month of May last, the plaintiff in this case proceeded to Tortola for the purpose of purchasing some goods which had been advertised for sale there as being saved from a wreck. On the morning after the sale, whilst engaged in one of the Public Offices in Road Town, he was arrested sans ccrcmonie. by the Provost Marshal, and taken before the said Stipe, who committed the gentleman to prison, where he had to remain until sufficient hail could he procured for his liberation. The only excuse offered þÿ which we consider no excuse at all þÿ for this extraordinary mode of proceeding þÿ is that the plaintiff had been concerned in a riot on the previous evening, þÿ because forsooth he happened to leave the house of an acquaintance, in company with a few other gentlemen, at a moment when a mob of renegades was gathered in that part of the town. As the case will come before a Jury in the early part of August, we refrain for the present from giving our opinion on it, but will take care to do so bye and bye. All we have to say just now is that this is a most unheard of proceeding, and contrary to British jurisprudence. þÿ The plaintiff has laid his damages at £,1000
sterling.
