A New York editor says he had an introduction last week to the heroine of the following sketch Mr. , a merchant, now residing in Philadelphia, who formerly lived in rather an extravagant style, was in the habit every Monday morning of giving his wife a certain sum of money for the table and other household expenses ; he never mentioned his business to his wife, and she, deeming him capable of attending to his own affairs, never inquired into them. About five years after their marriage, through some slight mismanagement and the rascality of his clerk, Mr. suddenly broke, and his fall was mentioned "sympathisingly" on 'change,' and, like all such other matters, there all sympathy ended. The merchant kept the affair, a secret, and the first intimation his lady had of it was a news paragraph in the Ledger. Shortly after dinner was over, on the discovery of this startling fact, Mrs. requested her husband to re-

main in the parlour a few minutes, as she had something to say to him. She left him, hurried up stairs, and shortly after returned with a splendidly-bound Bible in her hand. Handing it to her husband, she said, " George, the day after our marriage you gave me this precious hook as a token of your love, and as a rich fountain to look to in the day of trouble. Its pages have been precious to me, arid as your brow looks sad to-day I now return it to you, that you may glean from it some consolation in the hour of gloom." She then left the room. The merchant opened the hook carelessly, and a bank bill fell out. He picked it up and looked at its face þÿ it was a ten dollar hill, lie opened the book again, and another note of the same amount was before him. He opened it at the first page and continued to find a note between every two leaves till he arrived at the commencement of the Book of Revelations. He was saved, could commence business, and had a capital of 6,000 dollars to start with. þÿ lie rang the bell þÿ a servant appeared. " Request your mistress to come to me immediately," said the merchant. The lady obeyed, entering the room with something between a smile and a tear. "Kate! Kate! where did you procure all this money V" "This is the weekly savings of our household expenses for | t the last five years," was the modest reply. " Every week I put ten out of twenty dollars which you gave me into our Bible bank, that when a day of trouble come upon us we should have something to save us from the wolf." þÿ

"But why put it in the Bible, Kate?" " Because it is a good hank, one which will not suddenly break," replied the lady. " You are an angel Kate," cried the delighted husband clasping her to his heart. And so she is. Does any one doubt it ? There arc thousands of' such angels, despite the railings of miserable woman-slandering bachelors.

THE WONDER OF THE DAY. In everv respect, and the least in the important one of finance, the Great Exhibition is a great success. The building is daily traversed by some thirty thousand people, to whom the impression conveyed of its grandeur, beauty, and utility, is hut a feeble type of the good it will far more widely diffuse. It is not for the mere pleasure of a holiday that in this very centre of the world's commerce, as (according to 8ir John llcrschell) of the world itself, the remotest and most various triumphs of human art and industry have been thus brought side by side. We would not make a party use of that to which all parties have nobly contributed; hut it is impossible to see such various products of industry brought together without thinking of the markets that await them, and of the wider freedom of intercourse they are meant to reciprocate and extend. It is, the plain moral of such a sight as this that all the parts and market-places of the earth must one day he open as our own, and that evcr\

impediment to commercial interchange, as to the inter-communion of invention and intellect, will be finally swept away. To view the space by the Eastern entrance appropriated to America, and compare its wealth of raw produce and poverty of skilled labour, with the departments immmediately adjoining so rich in labour and inadequate in produce, is to study a chapter of Free Trade more convincing than Adam Smith ever furnished. Hut to pass from the new world to the old, how singular and impressive are the lessons here conveyed to us of the races and destinies of man. The assemblage of wonders in the midst of which we stand is more than an exposition of the state of art of the nations of the wide world 'from < 'ilina to Per u.' Every one of them has contributed its most finished products, and the ethnology of the world may be read in the wondrous collection. And from till the surprising varieties of this astonishing scene may he drawn the solemn and instructive lesson of the still advancing progress of the human race, 'resulting from the common labour of all men,' variously retarded til various times but never finally stayed. Hut let lis not close this hasty glance at the wonders of the Exhibition without a mention of its greatest wonder. 8uc.ii in our judgment is the casket which enshrines till the rest, the Crystal l'a lace itself, finished in six months time, and of which nearly the whole materials whereof it is composed were probably crude and unformed, in the bowels of

the earth a short year ago. Mow many previous inventions, discoveries, and improvements were indispensable to this achievement! Without Watt's improvements in the steam-engine it could not have been done. It could not have been done without the improvement of the manufacture of glass. A\ ithout Sir Hubert Peel's hold and libera! measure of sweeping otf the pernicious excise from glass, it could not have been attempted. This was Sir Robert's own remark on the day of his fatal accident, when the plan we first submitted to him and bis fellow Commissioners; and it may increase even the bitterness of regret for the death of the great statesman, that lie should not have lived to see the structure accomplished in w hich at once he took so lively an interest. þÿ The Crystal Palace is a perfect structure. Its form is graceful, almost aerial, vet at the same time solid and substantial. It harmonises with the blue sky above it, and with the green earth around it; and, above all, its adaptation to its use is perfect. Taking all the circumstances into account, this structure of six months' labour may be pronounced without hesitation as a triumph of art and science more wondrous, with reference to means and ends, the need and the fulfilment, than the temple of St. Peter's, which it took three centuries to complete. The Crystal Palace took six months in building and cost one hundred and fifty thousand pounds ; St. Peter's took three centuries and cost sixteen millions. It is an honour to our

«THi <A % © m at AT13, country and age that such a fabric could not have been raised, either in the same time, or in any time, by any other race of men, or in any other age. We are not a brilliant people, hut we are a sure þÿ let us say, even a great one. The next achievement of thejvind will probably be accomplished by the same race of men on the opposite shore of the Atlantic; hut the time for that giant in the cradle to accomplish it has not yet arrived and without impatience he must await his manhood. And now a word for the parties under whose direction, management, or labour the great exploit of this Great Exhibition has been achieved. Our thanks and gratitude are due to all of them, from the Prince to the artiznn. If Nelson had been as good a judge of a glass palace as of a sea fight, he would certainly have pronounced without hesitation that every man of them had done 'his duty,' which, in this England of ours, is saying everything. Two of the parties in question, however, are pre-eminently entitled to distinction- þÿ the Prince, and the selltaught architect; the first for originating the design, and for his courageous perseverance in carrying it out, against the remonstrances of titled hut timerous obstructives, harassing!' persevered in down to the last moment ; þÿ and the last for the genius, which, in rising to the occasion above his ordinary daily pursuits, has at once done honour to his country, and to the people from w hom lie is sprung. þÿ English Paper.

An Amusing Scene. þÿ While the Court was in session at Paris, Lamar County in of Texas, a few weeks since, a robbery was committed at the Hotel of Mr. Tucker, which was attended with most ludicrous circumstances. The hotel at the time was filled with lawyers, litigants, witnesses, Ac., who bad retired to their beds and after a night of profound slumber, awoke every one of them coatless and pantaloonless. Some daring thief had made his way into their sleeping apartments and carried oil' every article of clothing belonging to each individual in the house. The Bonliam advertiser states that when the fact was known, a series of tableaux vivant, of the most ludicrously interesting nature, were offered by the garmentlcss lodgers the sufferers them-

selves laughing long and heartily at the ridiculous figure each other cut while shying and dodging about in search ot" their missing clothing. It was not long however, before the missing garmenst were found stacked in the public square, whither the burglars had carried them ; and now come the serious feature of the þÿbusiness every pocket had been rummaged, every red cent taken, all was empty. Several emigrants had lost, all their money, and the lawyers attending the court were reduced to a par with the clients who had the day before lined their pockets for tlicm. Some four hundred and odd dollars was the net profit ot that particular night's work to the enterprising projector, who got entirely off, undetected.

During the course of our operations we have very unexpectedly come across a Coral Shoal at the entrance of this harbour, having only 204 feet water on it a low tides. It stands directly in the fairway and is a danger of some consequence. The shallowest part of the shoal extends in about a north and south direction from 80 to 100 feet, and east and west front to 30 to 40 feet. It appears to he of coral formation, and full of inequalities, from the lead dropping olT the surface of the rocks into 5 and 5% fathoms. Beyond this nucleus of the shoal, the coral extends sixty fathoms to the westward, with depths of from 26 to 28 feet, and about forty to the eastward, having 28 to 30 feet, and oci asionally 34 feet. No exertions of the firemen could stay the progress of the flames in this warehouse, | and after burning for more than four ' Russia had a narrow' escape from des hours with undiminished force, they at length exhausted themselves, and at one

TRANSLATION. H E FREDERICK the SEVENTH by the Grace of God King of Denmark, of the Vandals and Goths, Duke of Schleswig, Holstein, Storniarn, Ditmarch, Lauenburg and Oldenburg. Our special favor ! By letter patent of this day's date We have most graciously made known to Our loyal subjects in Our West India Possessions Our Royal intention to cause some well informed and respectable persons to consider and report upon a draft of a Colonial Law for said Possessions. We therefore most graciously command Yon, on Your arrival in the Islands, to direct the several Burgher Councils to elect as soon as possible, each in behalf of its own Island, men qualified for the above purpose, four for St. Croix, three for St. Thomas and one for St. Johns, whereupon You will select two men, whom You, on mature consideration, mav deem

JIM 1851. well adapted to complete, in behalf of all the Islands, the election of the Burgher Councils for the purpose aforesaid. These ten men will then have to meet at Christiansted, on a day appointed by You, and after having been made acquainted by You with the contents of the draft of the Colonial Law for the Danish West-India Islands, ol which draft a copy is enclosed, it will be the duty of these men, presided over by You, to consider this draft and submit to Us their report on the same. As soon as You shall have received this report You will have to transmit the same, with Your own remarks, to Our Minister of Finances, who will refer it to Us for Our further decision. You will attend to the despatch of this matter, in such a manner, that the final draft of the Colonial Law may as soon as possible be laid before the Diet, assembling in the Autumn of the present year. Commending ftrou to the Grace of God. VVilmer X Smith' Time, Liverpool, June 16. Hamburgh lias been the scene of a serious riot, in which the Austrian soldiers were called out and fired upon the people. Eight persons were killed and eighteen wounded. The Austrian troops quartered in the suburb of St. Pauli, with field guns charged and primed, and the exasperation of the people at Hamburgh and Altona, is wound up to the highest pitch. There is very little news from the rest of Germany. The King of Prussia has returned to Berlin, w hich city has been the scat of rejoicings at the inauguration of the statue of the Great Frederick. There has nothing important yet transpired with reference to the congress at OImitz. The report of the appointment of M. Gonzales Bravo as Minister of Spain to Washington in contradicted. The Duke of Saldanha, contrary to expectation, is pursuing a wise and prudent course in Portugal, and he is endeavouring to conciliate moderate men. The Septembrists, however, count upon his versatility of character, and hope to overthrow him ere long. A decree has been issued for the dissolution of the Cortes, and for convening a new Parliament on the 15th of September next. þÿ There is an unaccredited report, coining through Paris from Madrid, that a movement against Saldanlia has suddenly burst out in Portugal, and that several regiments and the whole province of Estreniadura has declared for the Queen against the revolutionists. The rumours to which we alluded last week, which have their origin in Madrid, respecting counter-reactionary

movements in Portugal, have been industriously repeated, but nothing has occurred in the Peninsula beyond the usual intrigues of the two courts. The Right Hon. R. Pakenham, formerly our respected envoy at Washington, proceeds immediately to Lisbon as English Ambassador extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary. The Spanish Government is evidently desirous of a pretext to interfere in the affairs of Portugal. It is expected that the pregnancy of the Queen of Spain would be announced ollicially on the 10th July. The Sir Robert Peel screw steamer brings the latest news from the Cape, having left the colony on the 2nd May. Although the details of operations round King William's Town are very long and diffuse, when brought to the test of military examination, they add very little to what we gave last week. Sir H. Smith, shut up still in King William's Town, only dares to venture upon parate neighbourhood ; these " patrols," predatory excursions in the immedihaving for their object to harass and distress the enemy by the destruction of his crops and the capture of his cattle ; but the effect of this warfare is only limited to the spot. In some partial encounters in other places, when the Kaffirs can be brought to bay they have been vanquished ; but again these successes cannot have much effect on the issue of the war whilst Kreili and his allies are in the field. Some of our troops have arrived at the Cape, but the Vulcan, with the chief reinforcements, is still out. It appears still doubtful

whether Sir II. Smith will have sufficient force to cope with the enemy, and there is a report that a second regiment of cavalry will be dispatched forthwith. The sooner the better; since the only chance of bringing the Kaffirs to terms will be 'lie exhibition a of an adequate ff.r.e. P a cry ikely that the chiefs

are sick of the war, but these reports come filtered through our own camp; and until Sandilli and Kreili are hanged there will be no real peace. We are not surprised to hear that the missionaries are getting into had odour, being suspected of having taken the natives and of fomenting part with the war. One of these gentlemen has been seriously threatened at King William's Town, and has left for the Cape. We have news from India by way of Trieste to the 14th of May from Bombay, and from llong Kong to the 23rd of April. India was tranquil, but the western frontiers were still kept in terror by the robber bands in that locality. The news from Buenos Ayres is once more of a warlike character, and all the neighbouring powers are leagued against Rosas.

Arrival or Hungarian Refugees. þÿ The Peninsular and Oriental Company's steamer, Sultan, arrived, on Thursday, at Southampton. Among her passengers were the distinguished Hungarian Lieutenant-General Loizar Messaros, fortynine other Hungarian officers, and forty Hungarian soldiers. M. Francoes Izsollosy, Kossuth's Secretary, was a passenger on board the Sultan, from Constantinople to Malta, hut he was left at the latter in consequence of his being in ill health. Messaros took leave ofKossuth at Kutayah, on the 6th of May last. þÿ Christiansteds Vendue Office the 7th The great Magyar was then in bodily health, hut much broken in spirit, owing to his long captivity. He has again been promised his liberty, in September next, by the Turkish Government; but faith has been so repeatedly broken with him, through the machinations of Vustria and Russia, that there is no certainty when he will he suffered to go at fund lie folgende Sager til Politiekammeurge. Messaros is a tall, handsome man, bald-headed, with an immense beard. As soon as he landed from the Sultan, he waited on the Mayor of Southampton, to ask if any assistance could be rendered, in this country, to his compatriots, some of whom were destitute. He stated to the Mayor, that they had been treated with the utmost

kindness by the captain, officers, and crew of the Sultan. It was affecting to see this man standing before the Mayor, with his head uncovered, and with a voice trembling with emotion, beseeching hospitality. <iisi!vr!Ai\i\fi>, m Mr. EDITOR, The enclosed article is offered you for insertion in the columns of your paper, as it contains the sentiments of many of your fellow citizens, who gratefully appreciate the gracious intentions of 1 J is Majesty towards His Colonies. Respectfully. S. St. Croix, 12th July 1851. The right meaning of the word Freedom, a understood liy a loyal subject and virtuous citizen. Freedom, in the best sense of the word, is really a most estimable blessing. But the na'tiral man mistakes its real character. He supposes it to consist in what he calls Independence ; or, in other words, in governing and leading himself, according to Ids own ideas. Each one feels, in his own mind, that he has a right to control his own ways and he master of himself ; and hence lie is jealous of governments and authorities, especially where they seem to encroach upon his favorite delights. The fact that governments, in the present disorderly state of the world, so frequently abuse the trust placed upon them, confirms him still further in his jealousy ; for it makes it seem so much the more perfectly well-grounded : and the idea does not fail to enter, t lint government itself is an evil, and that a better state of society could be organized without any of its artificial forms. But an intelligent mind must see that all attempts to harmonize the social body, by the destruction of the bands which hold it together, and make it a society, are not merely inconsistent, but contradictory to reason. It must be

seen that order, on which harmony and union depend, cannot he promoted by multiplying sources of disorder, in giving still more free play to the disorderly passions of men, unrestrained by law, authority, or conventionality. The freedom which will bless men and make them happy, is not a state in which each shall be governed only by bis own independent will, which the selfishness of each will not fail to convert into a scene of perpetual strife between so many diverse, discordant wills, but one in which all shall he united, by a common love of mutual usr, more and more in the harmonious furtherance of a common good; and in which the less wise, acknowledging the superiority of the wiser, shall give up willingly to them the direction and oversight of the public good, as the best means of its being properly promoted and cared for. The uses of governing, teaching, and leading, ran, from their very nature.

1 1 «ic jit-i ss»i. properly he the business of comparatively few. And we find, accordingly, that there are, in fact, but few who are really capable of exercising well these functions. It is true, that every one has by nature more or less of the desire to lead, teach, and govern himself; and is impatient of the control and leading of others, so far as it is felt as a restraint. It is nevertheless true, also, that very few do exercise an influential governing power over others; and in a republic, however democratic it may professedly he, the many are as really led and controlled by a few (only in a different manner,) as under a monarchy. It is not left to men to choose whether they will he governed or not þÿ it is only granted them to choose whom they will serve, and by whom and by what principles they will be governed. The wisest man is not so much a man who knows enough to govern himself, as one who knows to place himself under the government of the noblest and truest principles; the most free is not he who is most independent of law, hut he who feels the least restraint from conformity to law. Ilence, when man founds his idea of true freedom upon the idea of an equality of conditions, of functions and of privilege, he takes a widely mistaken path. All are not capable of the same functions ; all could not occupy with advantage the same conditions; all could not equally profit by and enjoy, and would not equally deserve, the same privileges. Taking this for a basis, we find substituted for equality of condition, pri-

vilege, rights, and functions, þÿ an apportionment state, privilege, of and use to each, in precise accordance with his peculiar genius and ability, þÿ a place provided for each according to his capacity to fill it, instead of being awarded according to some imaginary scale of advantages which all are to share, whether they can enjoy and use them or not. When the time for the adoption of this principle will come, we are unable to predict ; but we safely may predict, that man will not have learned to be truly happy, either in his individual, social, or political Condition, until he shall have ceased to seek his happiness in the attainment of a position in which he can equal or rival his neighbour, whom he supposes more fortunate than himself, and shall rather endeavour to find it in a station which his families best enable him to fill, for which his genius and education have best fitted him, and in which he can make himself in all respects most vfful-
From the St. Thomas Times. M E M O 11 I A L to the RKJSDAG O F DEN M A R K.

We, the undersigned Inhabitants of the VVest India Islands, St. Thomas and St. John, beg leave most respectfully to present to the Rigsdag of Denmark, this Petition, praying that just and equitable compensation may be granted us for the loss we have sustained in our property, in consequence of the Ordinance of the Governor-General, bearing date 3rd July 1848; by which he took upon himself to abolish Negro Slavery in the Danish Golonies, and which act received the ltoyal sanction on the 22nd September of the same year. If notwithstanding the heavy loss thus sustained, we have hitherto been silent, it should be attributed to the hope we had entertained, that Government, without being called upon to do so, would have token steps to obtain compensation for us ; and to the sentiments of sympathy with which we beheld the struggle of the Mother Country in the trying situation in which the revolt of the Duchies, arid war with many powerful enemies had placed her, a struggle which required all her resources, both intellectual and material, of which she could dispose; and, thus it would have been inopportune had wc at that time obtruded ourselves on the notice of Government. Rut now, that the clouds which obscured the political horizon have been dissipated, now, that a glorious war is concluded, and peace sheds its blessings over Denmark, we can no longer defer our just demand for compensation, lest our silence should be construed into acquiescence with the act, by which we have been despoiled of our property, or in-

terpreted as an abandonment of our claims. We had as good a title of property to our negroes, as to our land, houses, or any other property we possess, this right was established not only by law, but the Government had moreover encouraged the subjects acquire to such property as being advantageous to the State. l'"or this purpose Government granted loans to the Colonists upon reduced interest from the so denominated Negro loan." þÿ " Government bought and sold such property, took it in mortgage, levied duties upon their importation, and imposed a yearly capitation Tax ; consequently not a shadow of doubt could exist of the legality of such properly ; and if it was a fault to become possessors of such property, it must be laid to the charge of the Government which had fostered and encouraged it. The highest tribunal of the land, the King's high Gourt acknowledged this right in its fullest sense, so that a negro slave, even on the free soil of Denmark, continued to be the property of his master so thoroughly, that the latter in direct opposition to the slave's will, could oblige him to return to the West Indies. That the negro's ability to work, and personal qualities enhanced his value, is a fact too palpable to stand in need of proof; the numberless legal appraisements upon oath, the sales which took place daily between man and man, as well as the normal value, which according to the Ordinance of the 1st of May 1840, was determined every year by the Government, after a previous hearing
of the Rurgher Council and the respective authorities, render this matter incontcstible.

JIT This Ordinance admits the owners' right to full compensation, for only on condition of paying the full value of the services which the master could have from his slave, had the slave the right to demand his freedom ; but without such remuneration his master could not be deprived of him. The forementioned Ordinance, the common law, and in particular the 87 of the constitution, lay down as an invariable rule, that no subject can be compelled to cede his property, unless the general good of the common wealth requires it, and then only on receiving full compensation. Those civilized nations in whose colonies slavery has been abolished, have neither raised any question or doubt as to (he legality of the principle of compensation. Thus England, i' i a nee and Sweden have gianted compensation. The first £25 12s. 6d. Sterling at an average per head. The second 490 francs per head, which is however considered but part of the whole sum, and the third in the following manner: 1st class, under 15 years, $80 per head, 2nd class, from 15 to CO years $240 per head, 3id class, over CO years $40 per head. With regard to emancipation without compensation the following language was field to the King of Sweden þÿ " Your most gracious Majesty, " in your high wisdom, will never allow such " a violation of justice, as emancipation with- ' out compensation would be, such a thing " lias never any were occurred." The Dutch Government has declared that it will not abolish slavery without indemnify-

ing the owners, and for this reason it has not given any formal sanction to the liberty which the Dutch Governor of St. Martin (with the consent of the planters) found himself compelled to concede to the negroes when emancipation was proclaimed in the French part ol the same Island, but left matters in statu quo. Once however, there existed an instance of emancipation without compensation: The national convention of France, in the year 1793, did disregarding the sacred rights of property, proclaim the abolition of slavery ; but 10 years afterwards, on the 28th May 1802, that act was declared, by the Corps legistatif, to be an act of spoliation, and as such illegal ; consequently slavery was reestablished by decree of the First Consul, and continued for half a century, and would in all probability be still in full vigour, at least for some time, had it not been for the revolution of February. For us, we have the most implicit reliance on the honor ol the Danish Government, and the Danish people, and wo feel persuaded that they will not follow the example of the National Convention. In Denmark, love of justice, and respect for the sacredness of the rights of property, are too deeply implanted in the soil to be easily rooted out. The proverbial honesty of Denmark is as firm as the courage, loyalty and gallantry, of which her sons have so lately given such signal proof. The Rigsdag of Denmark will not on account of the burden shrink from the demands of justice: it will not allow it to be

said that it refused to satisfy a claim, the justness of which has never been doubted by any civilized nation, nor will it sufler a number of its fellow citizens to be illegally bereft of their property without compensation.

The Rigsdng of Denmaik will not leave it in the power of the world to say that it was liberal at the expense of others, or that it denied compensation to the weak, because they had only the right, but not the power, to enforce it.

In reviewing the means that present themselves. the burden will not he so considerable or so heavy, when we take into consideration that the State possesses many plantations, in respect of which to their former compliment of slaves, there will of course be no question of compensation, and that it also holds mortgages on many properties, where the compensation can be written off', without any real loss in many eases; on the other hand the realm, by fulfilling its duty in settling a lawful claim, will gain by the disbursement of the compensation, which will, as may reasonably be expected, not alone increase the prosperity of the Colonies, but their inhabitants will attach themselves more closely to Denmark. We do not entertain any doubt but that the Rigsdag wiil grant us the compensation to which we have the most incontestible right, and which cannot be controverted hv such futile arguments, as, that the owners have lost nothing by the Government depriving them of their property, as the stock of labour is the same, and to be had for an equitable hire. If it even in reality were the case, that the expences were not greater and the work not less than before the emancipation, while, alas ! the contrary is the case, it would nevertheless be a species of argument in itself contrary to common sense, in a degree, that it would scarcely require any refutation at the bar of the enlightened Rigsdag, as it might with just as much reason bf said, that all the rest of the property of peo-

ple could be taken away whenever the Gov. ernnient managed matteis in such a way, that the properties could be tented at so moderate a rate, that the expenses did not exceed w hat those of the keeping of the property yearly had amounted to. It will be clearly evident that the owner, notwithstanding, loses his essential rights, for the property would no longer be at bis disposal, or under his control , he would be dependent upon others, not onlv as to renting of that kind of properly, of which he hud formerly been possessed, but he would not be able to sell, mortgage, or dispose of it in any manner whatever, either in favor of himself, his children, or other þÿheirs, in short, property would to him entirely lose its money value, and the capital vested in it would be sunk as is now the case with us.

Many a slave owner derived his living from the yearly income which the hire of his slaves produced, but now the State has bereft him of his property, and hurled him, Widows and Orphans, into the most abject poverty and misery, while that act as yet without compensation has, more or less, generally affected those who possessed that class of property, and in numberless instances property produced pecuniary embarrassment, while the slave owners who are proprietors of plantations have not alone lost the capital invested in their slaves by the subversion of the ancient normal order in the Colonics, but in addition thereto, they are exposed lo the imminent risk of seeing their Estates, Ruildings and Fabrics eventually reduced to no value whatever. Most assuredly the circumstances which preceded the emancipatioo
a N

cannot bo brought forward in support of the necessity thereof; such a delusion cannot hold good. It is notorious that the so-called insurrection which was begun in the jurisdiction of Frederichsted at St. Croix, on the 3rd of July, 1848, would have been put down, if the forces þÿ although reduced as they had been had been called out and ntade use of | þÿ by the Government of that Island This is borne out by the sentence of 5th February, in this year, rendered against the Governor- General, by the Commission, which sentence expressly states that the declaration of emanipation partly originated in a desire to promo the Treasury an exemption from compensation, or what is the same thing, it was mended to serve as a means to deprive the pioprietors of their legal right. Furthermore, it is quite evident, that even the most ; rifling commotion would not have occurred, :i the Capiain General of l'uerto Kieo's offer of assistance on perceiving the impending danger had been accepted ; neither is it less certain, that the normal order could have been re-established subsequently. His Majesty's Government by presenting to royal assent, the emancipation of the negro slaves, which the Governor General bad taken upon himself to grant, has adopted the act as its own. It has also from the very heinmiing been considered that t fie insurrecturn could not be viewed as a sullic.ient fouudation for the act. This is clearly to be .on from the wording of the Koval mandate n which the emancipation is made a conces-

sion " to the lively wishes of the negroes." That his late Majesty King Christian 8th, of glorious and blessed memory, had, by rescript of 28th July, 1847, given freedom to ail children born of slaves in the Danish f West India possessions, and at the same time oidained that slavery should finally cease in IV years, cannot be pleaded as a reason that proprietors of slaves are to sustain loss and to receive no compensation, lor the question remained open, and had been only glanced at by said rescript. It is much to be lamented that the emancipation in the manner it took place, and with the circumstances with which it was accompanied induced the slave population, although erroneously, to believe thai they had overawed the Government, and to receive the emancipation, not as a boon, hut rather as a trophy. The bad impression which such a management of matters has caused wiil ever remain, and render the march of the administration difficult ; tor defiance has taken the place, which only should have been ceded to gratitude.

It ougiit here to be observed, that a succession of Ordinances had gradually loosed the ties which existed between the master and the slave. What heretofore had been esteemed a favor on the master's part, was hv law converted into an obligation, and the slave was not only rendered more and more independent of his master, but his sentiments of attachment to him were destroyed. Thus, the Law made it obligatory on the master to cede a negro for his freedom, when he could pay his full value ; a favor which hardly any one had thought of refusing þÿ thus, the Law bound the master to give his slaves certain little extras for Ghrislmas ; a favor which no one had thought of denying, and thus, the Law compelled the planter to give his negroes the Saturday free, a boon, which

<8 & AD It X A T Jt & hitherto, frequently had been granted as a recompense for diligent work during the week. But from the moment that the Law converted into an obligation that which hitherto had been received as a favor, indifference usurped the place of gratitude. Thus, by consecutive innovations, the state of things became precarious, the relations insecure, impatience sprung up, and tbe seeds of the tumultuous scenes, which ensured and served as a pretext for emancipation, were sown. Here we must observe, that though it were admitted that the pretended insurrection at St. Groix, rendered emancipation, an act of necessity, it cannot, at all events, in any manner, be cited with tegard to St. riiomas, or St. John, where no kind of disturbance existed among the slave population. Thus, entertaining the intimate conviction that our right to compensation is as conformable to reason, as it ought to be sacred and inviolable, and in solemnly protesting against our being bereft of our property, without full compensation, we submit this our representation lo the Kigsdag of Denmark, with the most unlimited confidence in its justice. VVe have the consoling hope and encouraging persuasion that the Representatives of a people who, by the bill of indemnity, of 30th June, 1850, have gone ahead of, and set a brilliant example to, other nations, by the acknowledgment of the principle of equity that " all citizens ought equally to share the losses, whicti t he scourge of war I had brought upon individuals," will not deny
a principle of justice which every European nation has hitherto not neglected to comply with towards its Golonies. ISt. Thomas and St. John, Jii.nb 1851.

From the "Alta California." Iiitrrrting From Valparaiso. Terriri.e Earthuuake on the Coast. We have just received intelligence of the occurrence of one of the most alarming earthquakes that has visited Chili since 1822. At twenty minutes before seven o'clock on the morning of the 2nd of April, the inhabitants of Valparaiso were thrown into consternation by a tremendous shock which lasted about forty seconds. A great number of houses fell to the ground, and many others were materially injured. Of some the roofs fell in, and the walls of others were split in twenty different places, from the top to the base. Should there be another shock similar in violence and duration to the first, the whole city would be laid in ruins. During the three following days, slight shocks, were continually recurring to the constant alarm of the inhabitants, who, at each shock would rush out into the streets in apprehension of the falling houses. The town presented a most melancholy appearance, the streets being filled with people afraid to venture into their dwellings and terrified by a vague dread of what was to conic. þÿ When night approached, two-thirds of the population availed themselves of the protection of the vessels in the harbor. Some camped out on the hills and in the

market places. The shocks were felt on board the vessels, the sensation being similar to that caused by a ship grounding. Many houses that remained standing have been condemned as unsafe. The city of Santiago shared the fate of Valparaiso. The Cathedral and several of Ihc churches were considerably damaged ; and it is impossible to estimate the amount of property destroyed, inasmuch as almost every individual has suffered. It is not known how many lives were lost, but it is supposed the number is very small considering the violence of the shock and the downfall of so many buildings. When our informant left Valparaiso no accounts had been received from tbe coast, but it is altogether likely the shock was of equal severity in other places. þÿ - - Condition of Nicaragua.

The causes that arc operating here, and to which I have alluded, no not originate here, they are foreign. This country was hut a few years since almost unknown þÿ its vast capacity was only rumoured þÿ hut since the discovery of California, the anxiety of the people to find some short route to the land of gold, has led many across this State. In this anil other ways, the country has been opened to the knowledge of the public; and the American public have not been slow lo take advantage of facilities to be found here for accumulating wealth. Many Americans are here already, and many more are coming. A number have bought estates here, and arc entering into the cultivation of the products of the country. Resides this, the German Emigration Society is now making preparations to send a large number of people from the German States, most of whom have been engaged in the political movements of the last two or three years. This Society has been endeavoring to negotiate a grant of land from the Government, but as yet they have not been successful. They are intending, in case they succeed, to bring over from fifteen hundred to two thousand people. During lite past winter, as you know, large numbers of returning Californians have passed through this State on their way home. These men almost without exception, carry home good reports of the land. Many ot them have expressed tbe determination to return here, and some have remained here and entered into business ; most of them have pur-

chased land and are preparing to cultivate it. I his large number ot foreigners coming in contact with the natives has produced already quite a change in many of their notions, and the seed thus sown is working and will work until a thorough change is wrought in the character of the people. They arc now for the most part indolent, not disposed to produce more than is necessary to sustain life þÿ the comforts and luxuries bcin<r unsought. This national character is not to he overcome in a day or a year; hut time is sufficient to renovate this. Beside, ifgufli-

cient inducements are offered for immigration and people flow in here from civilized States, with the means and appliances of civilization 1 lie weaker must yield to the stronger; and as in every case where ignorance comes in contact with skill it must retire ; the probable destiny of the natives of the country would be ultimately extermination, and the soil would pass into the hands of those more capable of improving the gift of Heaven. Another cause which, even prospectively, is exerting a great influence here, is the Ship Canal. If this gigantic work is ever accomplished the influence it will have 011 this country will be no less remarkable than that it must exert 011 the Commercial relations of the world. These are a few of the influences at work in this country now; and, although they may not be very obvious, yet, nevertheless, they are producing their own results, þÿ results too, which must have a very important hearing on the future history of these States. We extract from the Musce des þÿ Families the following libellous passage, which lias been contributed by a Monsieur de Wey, whose name should be spelt Whey, as the milk of human kindness seems in his nature to have all curdled. Speaking of English costume, he audaciously says : þÿ " I.adies may he met with who are well dressed, although, generally speaking, a sort of audacity is displayed in wearing the most irreconcilealde colours. What gives English women a somewhat bizarre appearance, is the custom they have of swelling out their petticoats, by means of circles of whalebone or iron ; this causes them to resemble large hells in movement." þÿ Now we ask of any of our readers, who are in the least acquainted with the mysteries of female attire, it the above account be true 1 Do English ladies make use of any of the articles above mentioned? Is "whalebone or iron" ever used in any part of an English lady's dress? Are such hideous artifices ever exposed for sale in any of our shop-windows ? No þÿ it is a gross libel ' We never recollect seeing anything of the sort in Regent Street, of Ludgate bill, or the old Cranbourn Alley, or anywhere else, where bonnets, corsets, horse-hair petticoats, and all the accompanying charms of costume that make Lovely Woman so irresistible, are laid bare in their perplexing variety to the profane gare of Man. We mean to say, that the window which had the hardihood to disclose such abominations,

would be instantly smashed to pieces. If our Ladies are "great swells," at all events it is not produced by the insidious means of pipes and air-tubes, which Monsier Wey has endeavoured to insinuate, in such a roundabout manner, habitually hang round the graceful forms of our native beauties. In the name of the fair sex of our country, we declare that they are incapable of such hollow artifices. Monsieur Wey cannot rank amongst the polite ways of France, upon which his country generally prides itself, or else he would never have thrown out so base a calumny. If we had not so much to do, at this particular season ot the year, we would run over to Paris, and ask him what he meant bv it. þÿ lb.

As Mrs. M'Hibbon, a popular actress at Liverpool, was about to dress for Jane Shore, her attendant came to inform her that a woman had called to ask lor two box-orders, as she and " her daughter had walked four miles to see the play." " Does she know me ?" said the actress. " Not a bit," was the reply. " Very odd ; has the woman got her faculties about her?" said Mrs. M'Hibbon. "I think she has, ma'am," said the dresser, " for I see she lias got something tied up in a red handkerchief."

Cooper, in his novel of the slayer," makes some sport of a parcel of red Indians speculating over a chess figure, in the shape ot an elephant, which they describe as a beast with two tails. The incident really occurred in the case of an Irish servant at a country

house in Pennsylvania. A menagerie came along that way, and the elephant presented himself at the gate. The mistress of the house sent the servant forward with a feed of a loaf of bread. The " help" walked once or twice the length of the animal, and returned with the loaf. " Why havn't you given it to the elephant?" "Sure," says she, "and which end shall I give it to ?" " Hallo, steward!" exclaimed a passenger in an American steamboat, after having retired to his bed. " Hallo, steward!" "Here, massa," "Bring me the waybill." " What for, massa?" "I want to see if these bugs put down their names for this berth before I did; if not, I want 'ent turned out."
